title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
hook: "where was I before I was born?" the hymn's last two verses ask that question about everything, and end with "or perhaps"
carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta's fifth verse: a cord stretched across, and a question on each side of it. Was there below? Was there above? Which line did you ask about? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

Where was I before I was born? A small child might ask it at bedtime, wide awake, while the grown-up in the doorway searches for an answer. There are a few ways to handle it. Give a confident answer. Change the subject. Or sit down on the edge of the bed and say, honestly, that's a big one, and nobody has seen all the way back. The Nasadiya Sukta has been circling a bigger version of that question since its first verse. Now, in its last two, it asks it straight out. Today: who really knows?
screen: `WHERE WAS I BEFORE I WAS BORN?` → `A CONFIDENT ANSWER, OR A NEW SUBJECT?` → `OR: NOBODY HAS SEEN THAT FAR BACK.`

segments.voice: Verse six opens with a question. Ko addha veda. Who really knows? Who here could declare it, where this was born, where this creation came from? Then a startling line. The gods, it says, came after this world's making. They are on this side of it. So even the gods weren't there to see the start. Who, then, knows where it arose? Verse seven tries one more answer. This creation, wherever it came from, whether it was made or whether it wasn't, the one who watches over it in the highest heaven surely knows. And then the last words of the hymn: or perhaps that one does not know. In Sanskrit, so anga veda yadi va na veda. Readers have heard that ending in more than one way. Some traditional readers take it as a way of honoring the overseer: the beginning is so deep that only the highest one could know it, if anyone can. Some modern readers hear plain, honest doubt, kept inside scripture. Others hear both at once, a reverence that refuses to pretend. The hymn itself simply stops. It doesn't add a verse to tidy things up. It ends where a wise grown-up at a bedside might end: that's a big one, and here is how far anyone has seen. The question stays open, and the hymn is still sung.
screen: `KO ADDHA VEDA: WHO REALLY KNOWS?` · `THE GODS CAME AFTER THE MAKING.` · `THE ONE IN HIGHEST HEAVEN SURELY KNOWS.` · `OR PERHAPS DOES NOT KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sort what you've seen from what you haven't. Settle, and breathe. Bring up one thing you know because you were there: a face, a kitchen, a street you walked. Silently, call it seen. Then bring up something you only believe, or were told, or guess at. Call it not seen, gently, with no judgment. Go back and forth for a while, seen, not seen, letting each sit for a breath. Notice that both can be held in the same quiet mind. If you pray, you can offer the not-seen to God. The bell holds the time.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The hymn of creation. It ends: the one in highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps that one does not know. Today's word.

Your line: the Nasadiya Sukta, the hymn of creation, who really knows? Today, when someone asks you something you can't truly answer, try saying how far you've seen, and no further. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Hindu commentators and modern readers interpret the Nasadiya Sukta's closing 'or perhaps does not know' in different ways, and the hymn is still kept in traditional Vedic recitation.

original.note: Sanskrit: who really knows? The question that opens Rig Veda 10.129.6.

trapdoor: what you thought: scripture is where the questions get answered.
what it means: this hymn, kept as scripture, ends with its own question still open.
what a scholar hears: so anga veda yadi va na veda, 'he surely knows, or perhaps he does not know,' read by some as reverence and by others as honest doubt.

notes: Last Nasadiya day; tomorrow begins the Purusha Sukta. The teach recaps verses 1–5 as covered on 1250–1254. The practice was changed to avoid repeating 1251's carry (carry one big question without forcing an answer).
